coach_says: You're already a piece down, and Nh5+ doesn't change much: it is about as good as the alternatives. Simpler was Nxd5+, swapping off White's knight on d5, which is White's best piece and eyes e7 and c7. When you're behind, trading the opponent's most active piece is usually more useful than a check that sends your knight to the edge.
also: trade off the strong d5 knight

coach_says: Good: Kxc8 takes back the knight that just captured your bishop,, and it's the engine's first choice. Next, watch the bishop on c4, which is attacked by your d5 pawn while the e5 pawn and b2 are targets for your bishop.

Two pieces are hanging here: your knight on h4 (to the d8 queen) and Black's bishop on b1 (to your rook). Nf3 saves the knight but lets the bishop escape to e4, so you stay a piece down. Bb5 first pins the c6 knight to the king and gains time: if Black grabs your knight with Qxh4, Bxc6+ bxc6 Qxc6+ forks king and the a8 rook, and you can take on b1 next. When both sides have pieces en prise, look for a move that adds a threat before you recapture.
concept: pin with a threat before recapturing

coach_says: White's bishop on d8 is out on a limb and only held by the queen on h4. Be7 attacks the queen, but it lets White simply swap that stray bishop off with Bxe7, which untangles White's position. Bd6 was stronger: it guards c7, develops, and keeps White's queen and bishop awkward, so ...h6 and ...g5 can chase them while you get ahead in development. Don't offer a trade that rescues your opponent's badly placed piece; gain time against it instead.
also: gain time on the early queen

coach_says: In a rook endgame the king should march forward. Kf4 heads for e3, right into White's camp, where it supports your rook and cuts White's king off. Kf5 stays on the fifth rank and does less; after b4 your rook is kicked and White's queenside pawns get rolling, and your edge is gone. With rooks on, ask each move: how does my king get closer to the action?
concept: activate the king in the endgame

coach_says: Your knight on g3 is attacked by the bishop on f4 and nothing defends it (the f2 pawn can't take only because your c5 bishop pins it). g5 hits the bishop, but White just takes the knight first with Bxg3, and your g5 push has also loosened the squares around your king. When a piece is attacked, save it before counterattacking: Nf5 or Nh5 keeps your extra piece.

Your king is being hunted, and Kg7 walks back into Nh5+, after which h6 is the only square (h8 is blocked by your own rook) and Bc1+ continues the attack until you lose heavy material. Rf8 does two jobs: it clears h8 so your king can escape after Bc1+ Kg7 Nh5+ Kh8, and it attacks the f6 knight. When your king is under fire, look for a move that gives it a flight square or adds a defender instead of shuffling it back and forth.
concept: give the king a flight square

coach_says: Black's queen on d3 attacks your rook on f1 along the d3-f1 diagonal, and nothing defends it. Qf3 doesn't help (your f2 pawn blocks the queen), so Black takes Qxf1+ with check and you're suddenly losing. Before making your own plan, ask what the opponent's last move attacks: here Re1 or Rd1 moves the rook to safety and you stay clearly better.

Your b3 pawn is attacked twice (queen on b5 and the rook on b8 behind it) and defended only once by your queen. Ba7 attacks the rook, but Black just takes Qxb3, which also protects the rook along the b-file, so you've lost a pawn. Count attackers and defenders on your own weak pawns first: Qc2 guards b3 and hits c7 at the same time.

The g-file is open and your king is on g8. Bg5 attacks the queen, but after Rg1 the bishop is pinned to your king on the g-file, so it can't take the queen, and White wins it with Bxg5. Step off the open file first: Kh8 avoids the pin and then ...Rg8 fights for the file. Before putting a piece on a file or diagonal with your king behind it, check whether a rook or bishop can pin it.

You're up material, but your king is still on e1 with the e-file open and your own bishop blocking f1. c4 attacks d5, but it also gives up c3 as a block, so ...Qb4+ Rd2 Qb1+ Rd1 Qxe4+ wins your e4 pawn and then the h1 rook. When ahead, get your king safe first: Bb5 develops, gives the king f1 after ...Qb4+, and trades off the c6 bishop.

Black's queen on g6 is aiming at g2, and the only thing guarding g2 was your bishop on f1. Bd3 attacks the queen, but it takes that defender away, so Black just grabs Qxg2 and also hits your rook on h1. Before moving a piece, check what it was defending: Bg3 or Nf3 keeps g2 covered.

Your e5 pawn is under fire from the f4 pawn and the c3 bishop. a4 chases the b3 bishop, but White doesn't retreat: Bxe6 fxe6 fxe5 dxe5 Bxe5 wins the pawn. Deal with the central tension first, for example Bxb3 cxb3 and then ...Re8 to guard e5, before starting play on the queenside.

White has castled and your king is still on e8, so opening the centre now helps White. After exd5 exd5 Nxd5 Nxd5 Ng5, White hits f7 and the d5 knight at the same time (with Qf3 coming), and you lose material. Finish development first with Be7 and castling, then think about ...d5.

Black threatens Qxg2 mate: the queen on g5 and the knight on e3 both hit g2, and only your king guards it. h4 attacks the queen but does nothing about the mate. Always ask what your opponent threatens before attacking; g3 blocks the g-file and stops the mate.

Your king is still on e1 facing a rook on the open e-file, a queen and a knight. cxd5 grabs a pawn but allows Qb4+, and after Ke2 Nc5+ (discovered check from the e8 rook) it's mate in a few, while Rd2 runs into Qxd2 mate. Before taking a pawn, look at every check your opponent gets. Qd4+ was the move: it comes with check, brings the queen back to defend, and buys time for Be2 and Kf1.
concept: missed checks against your uncastled king

coach_says: White threatens Nf7 mate: the knight checks from f7, your own knight blocks h7, and the queen on g3 covers g8 and g7. a5 ignores it. After your opponent moves, always look for their checks first; Qh5 covers f7 and stops the mate, and you're still winning.

Both b7 and c7 are loose. Bxc7 wins one, but Black gets time to cover b7 and kick your bishop with ...Rc8. Qxb7 first comes with a threat on the a8 rook, so after Black saves it you can still take on c7 and come away with two pawns. When there are two things to grab, take the one that attacks something first.

You're two pawns down, but your rook is attacking h7 and Black's king is far away, so this should be a draw. Kg4 lets Black play h5 with check, and the g6 and h5 pawns then protect each other and roll forward. Kg2 or Kh2 keeps your king where the pawns can't check it, and you can take h7 next. In rook endgames, don't put your king where an enemy pawn can advance with tempo.
concept: let the pawn advance with check
also: king in front of the pawns

coach_says: Your knight on b5 is attacked by the queen, but Nxc7 saves it with a fork: from c7 the knight hits the queen on a6 and the rook on a8, so you win a pawn and then the rook on a8. Qb3+ only defends the knight and lets Black swap queens. When a knight is attacked, look at every square it can jump to, especially ones that hit two pieces.
